cells.tense: The direction holds, and the hands holding it are steady now.
cells.act: hold someone else up with what you have
cells.ask: Pick one person carrying something heavy this season and take one piece of it off them — a task, a shift, a call — and finish that piece yourself.
cells.core:
You know which way you're pointed, and the endurance underneath is doing what endurance does: it holds. The two run in the same direction — the aim keeps the standing steady, and the standing keeps the aim from scattering into ten possibilities. Nothing here needs defending or explaining, and on a given day you can tell whether you're on the line you set.

What this is suited for right now is being put under someone else's load for a while. The same strength that holds your own direction can hold one piece of someone else's life steady while they catch up. Choose one person and one concrete piece, and carry it through to done. Not a promise to be there forever — one task, finished, handed back.

cells.tense: The direction is already chosen, and the body is already braced against a weight not yet here.
cells.act: distinguish what is yours from what you borrowed
cells.ask: Name every pull on your direction right now — obligations, other people's hopes, old plans — and mark which ones are actually yours. Then close the page.
cells.core:
You've settled on the way you're going, and now you're carrying it like something that could be taken from you at any moment. The shoulders are up. The body rehearses a weight that hasn't arrived, and that rehearsal spends the strength the actual going would need. You can tell because the plans get more detailed than the days do, and the bracing feels like care.

Before the direction has to prove itself, sort what's really pulling on it. Every obligation, every hope someone else holds for you, every old plan still hooked in — name them and mark which are yours and which you took on from someone else's want. Then close the page. The list isn't a decision, just the load sitting where you can see it. Most of the bracing is against borrowed weight, and borrowed weight set down lets a direction move.

cells.tense: The direction was decided, and the hands that decided it are still standing where they chose.
cells.act: rest in the result of the tending
cells.ask: Take one hour this week with something you already built — a habit, a body of effort, a relationship — and stop adding to it. No improving, no next version.
cells.core:
The choice happened. The direction was set. Your body hasn't moved with it — you're standing at the threshold with the handle in hand, because holding is what you know and going is a different motion than holding. The strength goes into staying where the choice was made instead of into the going it asked for.

Rest comes before the going resumes. Take an hour with something care already produced — a practice you kept, effort that became a result, a person still in your life because of choices you made — and stop trying to improve it. Not a review, not a next-step list. Your body learns the direction is real by being somewhere the direction already took you. The going picks up once the standing stops. One hour, this week — that's the whole act.

cells.tense: The direction runs your days while your own account of it stays small — getting through, keeping up.
cells.act: share your strength where it is needed
cells.ask: The next time someone asks for something you can give — a hand, an hour, a straight answer — give it, and when they thank you, don't shrink it. Say you were glad to.
cells.core:
Something is shaping what you do, and your description of it is busy. People can sense it. They ask what you're building toward, and you answer with your schedule. The aiming is happening — it's just not being claimed by the one doing it, because a direction named out loud is one you could be wrong about.

What returns it isn't a speech. It's the smaller version of the same move: give what you have where it's needed, and when they name it back, don't sand it down. Say you were glad to. That's the entire correction — a strength received at its actual size instead of waved off. The direction doesn't need a declaration, just an honest answer the next time it's offered back to you.
cells.sheetLine: Something is steering you, and getting through is the name you give it.
cells.verb: choosing which light to steer by

attempts.check: The draft leans on the idea that the person's endurance is what carries their direction, but the record only says Fortitude is the seat the orientation landed in — it doesn't say the endurance is doing the work or that the direction has ever been tested. A reader could reasonably say the direction is clear and the body is simply tired, not that holding is the whole story. The asks survive that: each one is one act toward another person or toward one's own pull, useful even if the person is nowhere near a wall. The sentence that serves the writer more than them is about a weight only the body knows — I've cut it; the cell doesn't need that claim.
